callouts.text: Headline figures, read from the harness output rather than typed in. Nothing on this page is a hardcoded number.
The kill switch. Halting writes a file; the next ticket routes on R-00 and goes to a person with its draft attached. No deployment, nothing in flight lost.
Eight real tickets, each chosen because it takes a different route through the rules. The chip shows which rule will fire.
The routing decision, with the rule that made it and a reason written for a support manager rather than an engineer.
Intent with a calibrated confidence, meaning the probability this prediction is correct, and the runners-up it considered.
The passages retrieved, with their BM25 scores. Open a row to read the article the citation actually points at.
The reply as it would be sent. The [1] marker resolves to a passage above, and the closing paragraph tells the customer a machine drafted it.
A security incident, recognised with 100% confidence, and escalated anyway. R-01 is a policy rule: no confidence is high enough for this class.
Latency, the threshold that was applied, and which generator produced the text. All three go into the decision log.
The classification is confident and correct. It is not what decided the outcome, which is the point of putting policy ahead of confidence.
The handover note. Daniel, the tier two engineer, asked for exactly this: what the customer is asking, what documentation looked relevant, and what the system was unsure about.
The articles were retrieved and deliberately not sent. They travel with the escalation so the engineer does not start from a blank page.
Guardrails, recorded on every ticket. Grounding and the confidence floor read not applicable here because an internal note carries no citations and was never going to pass them.
